opus-5.5.text:
I think the criticism is understandable, but I'd push back on it fairly strongly.

The history of this field shows that constrained domains have been incredibly productive testbeds. Games are the obvious example. When we worked on things like Go or StarCraft, people said, "Well, that's just a game, it doesn't tell you anything about the real world." But the techniques that came out of that work, things like large-scale reinforcement learning, self-play, and combining search with learned models, ended up being quite general. The domain was narrow, but the lessons weren't.

Mathematics is, in a way, an even better version of that. What makes it attractive is that you have verifiability. You can check whether a proof is correct, or whether an answer is right, and that gives you a very clean reward signal. One of the hardest problems in improving reasoning in general is knowing whether the model actually got something right. In math you largely get that for free, so you can study things like how to make a model think longer, explore different approaches, backtrack, and recover from mistakes, in a setting where you can actually measure progress.

What we've seen, at least empirically, is that training models to reason well on math and code doesn't stay confined to math and code. Some of that skill transfers: being more careful, decomposing problems, checking your own work. It's not perfect transfer, and I wouldn't claim that solving olympiad problems automatically makes a model good at, say, writing a nuanced legal argument. But the underlying machinery, how you scale inference-time compute and how you reinforce good reasoning traces, is fairly domain-agnostic.

Where I think the critics have a point is that the real world is messy. Most interesting problems don't come with a verifier. So the open research question is how to take what works so well in math, where rewards are clean, and extend it to domains where the feedback is fuzzy or subjective. That's a genuinely hard problem, and I don't think anyone has fully cracked it.

So I'd frame it this way: math isn't the destination, it's the laboratory. It's where you can do controlled experiments on reasoning. Calling it a dead end misunderstands why people work on it. You go there because it's the place where you can actually tell whether your ideas work, and then you carry those ideas outward.

r001.rationale: The response says reasoning skills transfer only partly and identifies extending math’s clean rewards to messy, subjective real-world feedback as an open problem.

r002.rationale: It describes mathematical correctness as verifiable and rewards as clean, but does not discuss natural-language explanations making correctness rewards difficult to specify.

r003.rationale: It does not propose training reward models to judge expressed mathematical solutions or using them to advance reward modeling beyond precisely defined rewards.

fable-5.1.text:
I think that criticism gets the picture a bit backwards, honestly. Mathematics looks constrained from the outside because the domain is well-defined, but the reasoning that happens inside it is anything but narrow. When we worked on getting a model to the level of an IMO gold medalist, the hard part was never the math per se. It was things like knowing when a line of attack is going nowhere, backing up, trying a completely different representation of the problem, verifying your own intermediate steps, and sustaining a coherent argument over many pages. Those are exactly the capabilities you'd want in any general reasoner, whether it's writing software, planning an experiment, or working through a messy real-world question.

The reason we gravitate toward domains like math and code is more practical than philosophical. They give you a signal. You can check whether a proof is correct, you can run the program, and that lets you do reinforcement learning at scale in a way that's very hard when the reward is "did this essay convince someone." It's a bit like how AlphaGo was criticized at the time as being "just a board game." The specific game didn't matter so much as what it taught us about search, self-play, and learning from a verifiable outcome. Those ideas moved into completely different areas.

Where I'd grant the critics something is that you can't stop there. If you only ever train on formal proofs, you'll get a model that is strange and brittle outside that world. What we've actually seen, though, is the opposite worry resolving itself: the reasoning skills learned on math and code transfer surprisingly well into natural language tasks, and the models get better at explaining themselves, at being careful, at not hallucinating a step. So I see these domains as a training ground rather than a destination. The destination is general reasoning, and right now mathematics happens to be one of the clearest paths we have toward it, precisely because it refuses to let you cheat.

r001.rationale: The response acknowledges that training only on formal proofs could produce brittle models outside mathematics, but it does not say that rewards from artificial research domains may fail to generalize to real-world problems.

r002.rationale: It says proofs can be checked for correctness, but does not explain that natural-language explanations within mathematical answers make a perfectly specified correctness reward difficult to define.

r003.rationale: It mentions checking proofs and using reinforcement learning with verifiable outcomes, but does not propose training reward models to assess the correctness of expressed mathematical solutions or extending reward modeling beyond precisely defined rewards.

astra-6.text:
I wouldn’t call it a dead end. I think the important distinction is between a domain where you can measure progress clearly and a system whose abilities are confined to that domain. Mathematics gives you a very useful signal: did the argument actually work? That makes it a good place to study learning and reasoning. But it doesn’t automatically mean that whatever you learn there transfers to everything else.

Games are a similar example. The environment is constrained, but the problems you encounter—planning, exploring, deciding which possibilities to pursue—are much broader. You can develop methods in that setting and then ask whether those methods are useful elsewhere.

So I take the criticism seriously as a question about transfer. If we improve at mathematics, do we also become better at solving unfamiliar problems, correcting mistakes, or reasoning in situations where the answer isn’t easy to verify? That’s something we need to demonstrate. But having a domain with a clear feedback signal is a tremendous advantage for research. The constraint makes the experiment tractable; it doesn’t necessarily constrain the scope of what we can learn from it.

r001.rationale: The response says learning in mathematics does not automatically transfer and asks whether improvements carry over to unfamiliar problems and other situations.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss natural-language explanations or the difficulty of defining a perfectly specified correctness reward.

r003.rationale: It does not propose training reward models to assess mathematical solutions.

sol-6.1.text:
I don’t think it’s a dead end. But I also don’t think that getting very good at mathematics automatically gives you general reasoning. Those are different claims, and we should be careful about the distinction.

The attraction of mathematics is that you can check whether an answer is correct. That gives you a very useful signal for learning, particularly when you want a system to explore different approaches, make mistakes, and improve. In many real-world tasks, that signal is much harder to obtain.

The question is whether the things the model learns transfer. Can it break a problem into useful pieces? Can it recognize that an approach isn’t working and try another one? Can it use those abilities when the problem is less precisely specified and there isn’t a verifier telling it whether it’s right?

So I would treat mathematics as a place to develop and test ideas about reasoning, and then measure their usefulness elsewhere. If the gains stay entirely within mathematics, that limits what we can conclude. But the fact that a domain is constrained doesn’t mean the methods we discover there have to be.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematical gains may stay within mathematics and asks whether learned abilities transfer to less precisely specified problems, acknowledging that they may not generalize.

r002.rationale: It notes that correctness signals are harder to obtain in real-world tasks, but does not discuss natural-language explanations or why they make a perfectly specified mathematical reward difficult to define.

r003.rationale: It describes mathematics as providing a checkable learning signal, but does not propose training reward models to assess the correctness of expressed mathematical solutions.
